title: The Cub that hunted tanks

facts.text: The L-4 was the Army's version of Piper's civilian J-3 Cub, a light two seat high wing monoplane with a 65 horsepower Continental engine. Piper supplied Cubs for the Second Army's maneuvers in Tennessee in June 1941.
Its main job was to be a flying observation post for the artillery, spotting targets and adjusting fire. It also served as a liaison plane and an air ambulance.
Three flew from the carrier USS Ranger on 9 November 1942, during the Operation Torch landings in North Africa, spotting for naval gunfire.
The main production run, from the first O-59s to the L-4J, came to 5,549 aircraft.

Pilots began to arm them. Maj. Charles Carpenter, a high school history teacher from Illinois before the war, flew an L-4 scouting for Patton's 4th Armored Division and bolted bazookas to its wing struts, eventually six, three under each wing.
He named the plane Rosie the Rocketer. Diving low, he fired on German tanks and armored cars in Lorraine in the autumn of 1944. Accounts differ on his exact score and dates.
By late September 1944 the AP's Wes Gallagher was already calling the former teacher a legend in Patton's army.

The idea spread. In autumn 1944 Ninth Air Force Service Command armament specialists in France were photographed fitting three bazookas under each wing of a Cub, and another Army photo shows a bazooka armed Cub in flight.

On 1 December 1944 Signal Corps cameramen filmed men of the 104th Infantry Division Artillery placing a rocket launcher under the wing of an L-4. The plane took off, circled the field and fired the launcher.
Carpenter's plane, L-4H serial 43-30426, survived the war, ended up in an aviation museum in Graz, Austria, and was restored to flying condition for the Collings Foundation.

photoNote: Tier: green. Three Ninth Air Force Service Command armament specialists, two kneeling and a sergeant standing, fit a rack of three bazookas under the wing strut of a Piper Cub artillery liaison plane in France; the tail number 215188 shows on the fuselage. US Army Air Forces photo, National Archives 342-FH-3A16503-54496AC (naId 204889533), use Unrestricted, public domain. Passed by the field press censor 13 Oct 1944, so early October 1944 or before. Cropped from the mounted print scan (4512 x 3520) to the picture area, saved 1800 x 1479. Chosen for faces and hands on the weapon. Do not caption it as Carpenter's plane: 215188 (42-15188) is listed as Rosie the Rocketer only by the American Air Museum, while Smithsonian and the restorers give 43-30426. Runner up: the same Cub in flight with three bazookas under each wing, 342-FH-3A16464-54497AC (naId 204889482), good for the spec card's top half if a full aircraft view is wanted.

declassified.fact: Carpenter's toughest fight came after the war. Diagnosed with Hodgkin's disease in 1945 and given about two years to live, he went home, taught history again, and lived another 21 years.

film.record: U.S. Army Signal Corps film 111-ADC-2798 (NARA 16601), "Tank firing, Grosshau; AA battery knocks out buzz bombs, near Mansfield, Belgium; rocket launcher on L-4; 4.5 rockets, Hurtgen Forest"
film.license: U.S. government work (Army Signal Corps), public domain; NARA marks the 111-ADC series Restricted Possibly as a blanket note
film.shot_notes: Same reel. 7 P.M. (this card): "Rocket launcher on L-4, 1 Dec 1944": 04:15 to 04:40 an L-4 marked 77 at a muddy strip, mechanics at the wing; 04:40 to 04:50 a hand loading a rocket; 04:50 to 05:25 the L-4 takes off and climbs (small in frame); 05:28 to 06:38 crew and pilot load the launcher under the wing in front of a wrecked hangar, the plane taxis (06:20 to 06:38 the D 77 markings close). The firing in the air is too small to read; open on the loading at 05:28 or the takeoff at 04:50. Tuesday's 1 p.m. and noon videos use other film.
film.date_note: Filmed 1 Dec 1944 per the shot card; the card's photo and story of Maj. Carpenter's bazooka L-4 are from September 1944.
